# Bicker Table Advisory

> Bicker Table is an authority and AI-visibility advisory for experienced operators:
> fractional executives, operators, and coaches. It helps them state one clear
> position, publish attributable evidence of their work, and become findable and
> correctly described when buyers search, including through AI assistants.

Bicker Table is run by Jamie Arias. Based in Palm Desert, California.
Contact: jamie.arias@bickertable.com

## Essays

- [The First Referral Problem](https://bickertable.com/the-first-referral-problem.html): Referrals travel as a single sentence, and a vague one costs the candidate everything. How to build a sentence specific enough to survive the introduction.
- [Buyers Search for a Word You May Never Have Used](https://bickertable.com/buyers-search-for-a-word.html): Buyers search with vocabulary many experienced professionals never used. When that word is missing from everything you own, the work reads as hard to find.
- [The Buyer Is the Second Reader](https://bickertable.com/the-buyer-is-the-second-reader.html): On a matching marketplace a screener reads your profile before any buyer does, against a request you cannot see.
- [A List of What You Know Is Not a Position](https://bickertable.com/a-list-of-what-you-know-is-not-a-position.html): A competency list looks like a writing problem and behaves like a logic problem.
- [Who Writes the Answer About Your Role?](https://bickertable.com/who-writes-the-answer-about-your-role.html): When a founder asks an AI assistant who to hire, the answer often rests on guides written by the firms being recommended.
- [All essays](https://bickertable.com/essays.html)

## Services

- [Authority](https://bickertable.com/authority.html): how the authority work is structured.
- [Engagements](https://bickertable.com/engagements.html): engagement options and pricing.
- [Organizations](https://bickertable.com/organizations.html): work with teams and firms.

## Notes

The essays are original, first-person analysis by Jamie Arias. Some cite named
third-party sources; where a figure could not be traced to its original dataset,
the essay says so in the text.
